lines.text: Banks are central institutions in modern financial life, and understanding banking vocabulary is essential for anyone living or working in an English-speaking country. A current account (checking account in American English) is used for daily transactions — deposits, withdrawals, and payments. A savings account earns interest on money set aside for the future. Opening an account requires identification, proof of address, and sometimes an initial deposit. The bank issues a debit card for everyday purchases, and customers may apply for a credit card for borrowing. An overdraft allows spending beyond the account balance, usually with fees and interest. Bank statements — monthly summaries of all transactions — help track spending. Standing orders make regular fixed payments (rent, subscriptions), while direct debits allow companies to collect variable amounts (utility bills). Online and mobile banking have transformed how people manage money: checking balances, transferring funds, setting up payments, and receiving instant notifications. ATMs (cash machines in British English) dispense cash and accept deposits. Inside a branch, customers interact with bank tellers (cashiers in British English), personal bankers for advice, and mortgage advisors for property loans. Loans, mortgages, ISAs (Individual Savings Accounts), pensions, and insurance are key products. Understanding terms like APR (Annual Percentage Rate), interest rate, credit score, and terms and conditions is crucial for making informed financial decisions.

lines.text: British monetary vocabulary includes: 'quid' (informal for pound), 'pence/p' (penny plural), 'fiver' (£5), 'tenner' (£10). 'Penny-pinching' (being very careful with money) and 'in for a penny, in for a pound' (committed fully) are common expressions.
